Question: What is the quantum field theory for someone just starting to learn it?
Old_Answer: It’s a lot of math that’s fairly hard to learn, for one thing. Conceptually it’s not that awful - the basic process you go through is that you know what your “initial conditions” are (the particles you have coming in toward a potential interaction). You then basically guess at possible final configurations (particles created, annihilated, etc., and how they are behaving), and then you can calculate the probability of the initial config leading to that final config. You repeat this process for more guessed final configs, until the total probability you have accounted for so far gets close enough to 1.0 to suit you. If it’s well below 1.0, then there’s some final configuration you haven’t considered yet. That’s basically it. The math takes care of enforcing conservation laws and all other physical requirements. The big difference between this and classical physics is that you do not “calculate” the final configuration - you “propose it” (guess at it) and then see how likely that is. I assume that with experience you get better and knowing what final configs to consider. Stay safe and well! Old_Answer: This is a loose analogy, but consider a ball rolling down a hill. Basically it tries to find its way to the lowest point it can. If there’s a little extra low spot at the bottom of the valley, and the ball has much of a chance of getting there, it will. What it’s basically “trying to do” is shed as much gravitational potential energy as it can - trying to reach the lowest energy state. Irreducible representations are like “breakdowns” of a math structure that can’t be broken down any further. They’re kind of like the extra low spots at the bottom of the hill. It’s not energy we’re talking about this time, but when we do physics we try to make models of what’s happening in the world and we try to make those models as simple as possible. We try to “remove as much complexity” as possible. Well, if we can express something in terms more simple than we’re doing so far, we will - we like that. So it’s “our desire for simplicity” rather than “minimizing energy,” but there’s still the same sort of tendency for the models to become expressed in simpler and simpler terms. As far as why these representations are irreducible, well, everything has some kind of limit on how simple it can be. Take a golf ball flying through the air. In general, to describe it we need to specify its x, y, and z locations, and its x, y, and z velocities or momenta. That’s six numbers, and it’s as simple as we can get it. There’s no way for us to use five numbers, or four, and still fully describe the golf ball. The mathematical structure of the situation just requires a certain amount of “descriptive freedom” in order to cover all the cases we need it to cover. I hope this makes sense. Stay safe and well! So, to ensure that we capture all relevant information and respect the underlying symmetries, we stick to irreducible representations. Question: How does an electron "know" when it is the presence of another electron and not in the presence of a positron? Please don't tell me: "Oh, he detects the different charge".
Old_Answer: I’m very sorry, but that basically is the gist of it. Positrons and electrons are different particles with different attributes. These attributes, though, are really just labels we have invented to account for the different observed behavior. So, when an electron encounters either another electron or a positron, if it pushes that other particle away, that tells us that it has the same charge polarity as our electron. That’s the definition of charge, if you will. And if there is an attraction instead, that tells us that the other particle has the opposite charge. So it’s not so much that charge “causes” the force, as it is we assign the charge attribute based on our observation of the forces that happen. You could push down further - open up the quantum field theory bag, and find ways to use other, more sophisticated terminology. But ultimately it’s the same deal - we declare properties to be what they are because of how we see these entities behave. It pleases us very much that we’ve been able to identify patterns that are pervasive enough to give us a fairly simple labeling scheme. Ultimately, though, all we have is our perceptions of the world. All the equations, all the theories, all the properties - these are just things we’ve made up to tell us how we expect the world to behave in the future. Stay safe and well!
